Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the HealthBridge Hospitals third quarter fiscal 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. If you would like to register for a question, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HealthBridge Hospitals' financial results for the third quarter fiscal 2024. Joining me on the call are Dr. Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Jennifer Lee, Chief Financial Officer; Dr. Robert Kline, Chief Medical Officer; and David Patel, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that certain statements made during this call may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Dr. Michael Reynolds.

Dr. Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on our performance for the third quarter. We continue to execute on our strategic priorities, focusing on delivering high-quality patient care, expanding our network, and improving operational efficiency.

Today, I will provide an overview of our key achievements during the quarter, focusing on five key aspects: revenue per admission trends and drivers, same-facility volume and revenue growth guidance for the next quarter and year, status of ongoing or planned acquisitions and divestitures, impact of seasonality or external factors such as flu season, and trends in staffing levels and contract labor usage.

These areas highlight our disciplined approach to growth amid a complex healthcare landscape. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jennifer to provide a detailed review of our financial results and expand on these priorities.

Jennifer Lee:
Thank you, Dr. Reynolds, and good morning, everyone. As Dr. Reynolds mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Net revenue for the third quarter was $2.75 billion, an increase of 6.9% compared to the same period last year. This growth was driven by increased patient volume and improved payer mix.

Our operating expenses were $2.35 billion, representing 85.5% of net revenue. We are continuing to focus on managing our costs effectively while investing in key growth initiatives, particularly in supply chain efficiencies and labor management.

Adjusted net income for the quarter was $195 million, or $1.32 per diluted share. We are pleased with our financial performance and remain confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Now, let me dive deeper into those five key aspects Dr. Reynolds highlighted, starting with revenue per admission trends and drivers, which continue to be a bright spot in our performance amid a challenging macroeconomic environment. For the quarter ended September 30, 2024, our consolidated revenue per admission reached $15,420, marking a robust 4.8% increase year-over-year from $14,720 in Q3 FY2023. On a same-facility basis, excluding our divestitures in the Midwest, this metric grew even stronger at 5.2%, reflecting disciplined pricing execution, favorable case mix shifts, and operational leverage from our high-acuity service lines.

To put this in context, our total admissions for the quarter were 128,500, up 2.1% year-over-year, driven by sustained elective procedure volumes that are now 98% recovered from pre-COVID levels. This revenue per admission growth outpaced our peers—HCA Healthcare reported 3.9% growth in their Q3, while Tenet Healthcare saw 4.1%—and contributed approximately 60 basis points to our overall net patient revenue growth of 6.9%. Let me unpack the primary drivers, including case mix, payer dynamics, service line performance, and our revenue cycle initiatives.

Our weighted case mix index stood at 1.872 for the quarter, up 2.7% from 1.823 in Q3 FY2023 and sequentially flat from Q2's 1.870. This marks the fifth consecutive quarter of case mix index expansion, fueled by a deliberate shift toward higher-acuity patients. Key contributors include a 12% year-over-year increase in major cardiac procedures—such as complex PCI and TAVR volumes—and a 9% rise in neurointerventional cases, where we're leveraging our affiliation with the Southeast Neuro Center Network to capture more Level 1 trauma transfers. Orthopedics remains a standout, with joint replacement case mix index-adjusted volumes up 15%, benefiting from our robotic-assisted surgery program utilizing Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci Xi systems across 75% of our facilities.

We've also seen tailwinds from sepsis and respiratory acuity following the seasonal RSV uptick, though we're monitoring flu season closely. Importantly, this isn't just volume-driven; our clinical documentation improvement program, powered by 3M 360 Encompass and AI-enhanced natural language processing from Nuance's Dragon Medical One, has improved query response rates to 92%, capturing an incremental $28 per admission in DRG uplift. Without these technology investments, our revenue per admission would be roughly 2% lower.

Payer mix remains a core lever for revenue per admission. Commercial and managed care payers now represent 47% of our mix, up 150 basis points year-over-year, while Medicare held steady at 38% and Medicaid dipped to 12% following our selective contracting in high-cost states. This shift delivered 2.9% net revenue per admission growth from commercial contracts alone, bolstered by favorable unit cost escalators averaging 4.5%—ahead of the 3.8% industry benchmark from the Vizient Q3 survey.

On the government side, Medicare Severity DRG reimbursement under the IPPS final rule for FY2025—up 2.9% overall but with a -0.3% documentation and coding adjustment—pressured margins slightly, shaving about 0.5% off revenue per admission potential. However, our advocacy through the Federation of American Hospitals helped mitigate site-neutral payment risks from the Medicare Part B OPPS proposed rule, preserving inpatient revenue integrity. Medicaid redeterminations post-pandemic unwind have been a double-edged sword: while driving 3% admission growth in our Sunbelt markets, they've increased denials by 8%, which our denials management team—using Waystar's AI platform—has clawed back at a 75% overturn rate.

Regionally, this plays out differently. In our Southeast cluster (35% of beds), revenue per admission hit $16,850—up 6.2% year-over-year—thanks to robust commercial density in Florida and Texas, where employer-sponsored plans from Blue Cross Blue Shield and UnitedHealthcare have yielded mid-single-digit rate hikes. Contrast that with the Northeast (20% of beds), where revenue per admission grew a more modest 3.1% to $14,200, weighed down by New York and Massachusetts' regulated pricing caps and a 42% Medicaid mix. Our West Coast facilities bridged the gap at 5.5% growth, propelled by California Medi-Cal managed care expansions.

Beyond case mix and payers, revenue per admission benefited from optimized length of stay and ancillary capture. Consolidated length of stay compressed to 4.62 days, down 2% year-over-year, through our perioperative pathways and enhanced discharge planning via telehealth partnerships with Signify Health. This efficiency unlocked higher throughput without sacrificing acuity, adding $45 per admission in pharmacy and imaging revenue.

Service line commentary underscores our strategy: Surgical services drove 55% of revenue per admission growth, with outpatient revenue per admission surging 7.2% to $12,600 amid the shift to hospital outpatient departments ahead of potential 340B carve-outs. Cardiology revenue per admission climbed 5.8% on electrophysiology labs, while our oncology service line—bolstered by infusions from our biosimilars formulary—posted 4.9% growth despite oncology drug pricing reforms under the Inflation Reduction Act. Emergency department revenue per admission held firm at $2,450, up 3.4%, as we navigate observation stay scrutiny from CMS auditors.

We've invested over $150 million in revenue cycle management modernization this year, yielding tangible revenue per admission lift. Our Epic MyChart-integrated revenue integrity module has reduced clean claim rates to 97.5%—up from 94% two years ago—while automating prior authorizations via Availity's AI engine, cutting days in accounts receivable to 42 from 48. Charge capture compliance hit 98%, and our HCC risk adjustment coding for value-based contracts added $12 per Medicare admission. These efforts mirror HCA's revenue cycle management playbook but with our edge in regional data lakes, forecasting a 1-2% revenue per admission tailwind into FY2025.

Looking ahead, we expect revenue per admission to grow 4-5% in Q4, with case mix index stabilizing at 1.87-1.88 absent major flu or RSV surges. Risks include labor cost inflation—nursing wages up 5.2% year-over-year—and potential Medicare Advantage clawbacks, but offsets come from our $2 billion service line expansion pipeline, including 10 new neuro-ICU beds and ortho institutes modeled after UHS's success. We're also piloting bundled payments with payers like Anthem for joints, targeting 10% revenue per admission uplift through shared savings.

Moving to our second key aspect: same-facility volume and revenue growth guidance for the next quarter and year. For context, same-facility metrics exclude the impact of our recent divestiture of three underperforming facilities in the Midwest and the acquisition of two high-acuity hospitals in the Southeast, which we'll discuss separately. This keeps our lens squarely on organic performance across our core 180-hospital footprint, spanning 28 states with a heavy emphasis on high-growth Sunbelt markets like Texas, Florida, and Arizona.

For Q4 2024, we expect same-facility revenue growth of 5.0% to 6.0% year-over-year, building on the 4.8% growth we delivered in Q3. Admissions volumes should rise 2.5% to 3.5%, driven by a continued rebound in elective procedures and outpatient momentum. For the full fiscal year 2025, we're guiding to same-facility revenue growth of 4.5% to 5.5%, with admissions up 2.0% to 3.0% and revenue per admission expanding 2.5% to 3.0%. This outlook assumes no material deterioration in macroeconomic conditions, stable reimbursement rates from CMS, and continued execution on our operational playbook.

Diving deeper into volumes, inpatient admissions are projected to grow 2.5% to 3.5% in Q4, accelerating from 2.1% in Q3. This reflects pent-up demand normalization across orthopedics, cardiology, and oncology service lines, where we're now at 95% of pre-pandemic levels per our internal benchmarking against peers like HCA and Tenet. Surgical volumes, a key leading indicator, are tracking 4% higher quarter-to-date, fueled by our expanded partnerships with ambulatory surgery centers and a 15% uptick in total joint replacements. Case mix index should hold steady at 1.85 to 1.90, supported by higher-acuity neuro and cardiovascular cases.

Outpatient volumes remain our brightest spot, with expectations of 5% to 6% growth in Q4, mirroring the 5.3% we posted last quarter. Emergency department visits are up 4.2% year-to-date, bolstered by our AI-driven triage tools—similar to Epic's predictive analytics suite we've fully rolled out across 70% of our facilities—which have reduced door-to-doctor times by 22% and boosted conversion rates to observation or inpatient stays by 8%. Observation case growth is guiding to 3% for the year, as we're shifting lower-acuity patients to these higher-margin stays amid payer pressures.

Regionally, performance is bifurcated but trending positively. In our Sunbelt core—Texas and Florida, which represent 45% of our bed capacity—we're guiding 6% to 7% same-facility revenue growth for FY '25, with admissions up 3.5%. Population inflows from northern states, combined with our aggressive capacity expansions like the 50-bed addition at our Dallas-Fort Worth flagship, are key tailwinds. Florida's Medicare Advantage penetration, now at 42% in our markets, caps pricing but drives volume through our value-based care contracts with Humana and UnitedHealth, where we've achieved 92% STAR ratings. Contrast that with the Northeast and Midwest, about 20% of our portfolio, where growth moderates to 2% to 3% due to softer commercial reimbursement and nursing shortages. We've mitigated this with travel nurse reductions to 5% of our workforce—down from 12% last year—via our Bridge Academy internal training program, which has staffed 1,200 beds organically.

On revenue drivers, beyond volumes, we're forecasting 2.5% to 3.0% growth in revenue per admission for FY '25. This breaks down to 1.5% from net pricing, assuming flat CMS IPPS updates and modest commercial escalators in the 2-3% range. Payer mix stability is crucial here: Medicare at 52%, Medicaid 12%, managed Medicare/Medicaid 18%, and commercial 18%. We've clawed back 50 basis points of commercial denial rates through our revenue cycle management overhaul with R1 RCM, targeting a further 20 basis points improvement next year. Service line mix shift adds another 1% tailwind, with oncology revenues up 8% year-to-date on higher utilization of precision therapies like Keytruda and CAR-T, and neurosurgery growing 6% via robotics adoption—our da Vinci Xi systems are now in 85% of facilities.

Strategic initiatives underpin this guidance. Our Volume Velocity program, launched Q1 this year, has deployed capacity orchestration software from LeanTaaS to optimize OR scheduling, yielding a 12% increase in prime-time case utilization. Telehealth integration via our proprietary BridgeConnect platform—now handling 25% of initial consults—has expanded our catchment areas by 30 miles on average, particularly in rural Texas outposts. We're leaning into site-neutral reimbursement tailwinds; our hospital-at-home program, inspired by Mayo Clinic's model, is scaling to 15 facilities and projecting 2,000 episodes in FY '25, with 20% margins. On the cost side, supply chain efficiencies through our Group Purchasing Organization partnership with Vizient have held non-labor inflation to 2.5%, despite 7% drug price hikes.

Of course, risks loom. Labor costs remain elevated at 52% of revenues, though wage pressure is easing with national RN rates down 3% per Advisory Board data. Reimbursement headwinds from the Medicare 2.9% cut in the '25 IPPS final rule are baked in, but further sequestration or failed site-neutral legislation could shave 50 basis points off the low end. Seasonality in Q4—flu and RSV peaks—could add 1% upside to ED volumes but pressure lengths of stay if staffing tightens. Macro factors like persistent inflation or a softening employment picture might dampen commercial volumes by 1%.

Upside levers include faster elective recovery—our orthopedic waitlists are clearing 10% faster than HCA's peer average—and potential tailwinds from the Change Healthcare cyber recovery, where we've seen a 5% uptick in claims processing speed post our redundant Cerner Millennium implementation. We're also monitoring GLP-1 drug impacts; early data shows a 2% dip in bariatric volumes but offsets via increased GI procedures.

Next, on the status of ongoing or planned acquisitions and divestitures, which remains a cornerstone of our strategy to drive inorganic growth, optimize our asset base, and position us for the next phase of healthcare delivery evolution. In the hospitals and healthcare services sector, we're navigating payer mix pressures from Medicare Advantage penetration now at 42% nationally, supply chain inflation lingering at 5-7% for ortho and cardio implants, and a clear shift toward outpatient and value-based care models amid CMS's push for lower average length of stay and higher case mix index acuity.

Our disciplined approach to M&A is guided by three pillars: scale in high-growth markets, vertical integration into high-margin services like ambulatory surgery centers and inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and portfolio optimization through targeted divestitures. We've deployed approximately $1.2 billion in capital year-to-date for bolt-on and transformative deals, funded 60% through cash flow from operations—bolstered by our NOPAT margins hitting 14.5%—and 40% via low-cost revolver draws at SOFR + 125 basis points. Expect continued accretion: our pipeline targets 10-15% EPS uplift in Year 1 for tuck-ins and 20%+ for larger platforms.

On ongoing acquisitions, our flagship deal is the $675 million acquisition of Southeast Regional Health Network, a five-hospital platform with 1,200 licensed beds across Georgia and South Carolina. We announced the letter of intent in Q2 and closed Phase 1—three acute care facilities totaling 850 beds—on October 1st, just after quarter-end. This adds $420 million in pro forma annualized revenue, with a strong 28% EBITDA margin driven by a favorable 55/30/15 commercial/Medicare/Medicaid payer mix and top-quartile ortho volumes, up 15% year-over-year amid the Sunbelt migration boom. SRHN's facilities boast a case mix index of 1.92, well above our system average of 1.78, and we're already migrating them to our Epic platform for unified revenue cycle management, targeting $45 million in synergies over two years from shared services, procurement leverage via our GPO with Vizient, and payer contract harmonization.

Integration is on track: We've deployed our AI-driven denial management tool—powered by technology similar to Change Healthcare's ecosystem—which has already reduced days in accounts receivable by 4 days in the first month. Regionally, this bolsters our Southeast footprint to 22 hospitals, capturing 18% acute market share in the Atlanta MSA, where population growth exceeds 2% annually and commercial rates average 185% of Medicare. Expect full consolidation in Q4, with $0.12 EPS accretion in FY25.

A smaller but high-synergy tuck-in is the $180 million purchase of Coastal Ambulatory Partners, a network of eight ASCs and two inpatient rehabilitation facilities in Florida's I-4 corridor. Closing expected by year-end, pending Hart-Scott-Rodino clearance. This brings $95 million in run-rate revenue at 32% EBITDA margins—outpacing our hospitals' 25% blended rate—fueled by high-volume GI and ortho cases. Florida's ASC penetration is only 25% versus the 35% national average, so this aligns with our shift to site-neutral reimbursement strategies, especially as CMS's 2025 IPPS rule caps inpatient payments while boosting outpatient APUs by 3.2%.

Looking ahead, our $2.5 billion tuck-in pipeline is robust, with three letters of intent under negotiation and five in diligence. Key focus: Midwest expansion to diversify from our 65% Sunbelt concentration. We're advancing a $950 million bid for Heartland Critical Care Group, a four-hospital chain in Indiana and Ohio with 900 beds and embedded cardiology practices. Pro forma, this would add $550 million revenue, 27% margins, and critical IP cardiology service lines—ortho and cardio now represent 45% of our case volume system-wide. Strategic rationale? Midwest Medicare Advantage growth is lagging at 35% penetration, preserving commercial upside, and their average length of stay of 4.1 days complements our 4.3-day average, enabling bundled payment pilots under BPCI Advanced.

On the outpatient front, we're targeting physician practice platforms to vertically integrate amid the 20% year-over-year rise in employed physician models industry-wide, per MGMA data. A $320 million deal for Tampa Bay Oncology Partners—15 clinics, 40 physicians—would enhance our oncology service line, where margins hit 35% due to infusion revenue and 340B pricing. We've modeled $25 million synergies from Epic interoperability and our proprietary revenue integrity AI, which flags 98% of coding variances pre-submission.

Technical initiatives underpin these: Post-close, all targets get our telehealth stack—integrated with Zoom and Nuance Dragon for virtual rounding—driving 15% utilization growth, and our predictive analytics for staffing, cutting agency labor costs by 22% as we've seen in prior deals.

Discipline cuts both ways. We've divested $425 million in non-core assets year-to-date, generating $380 million in after-tax proceeds for M&A dry powder. Q3 highlight: Sold our two rural Kansas hospitals (220 beds) to a local non-profit for $210 million, closed September 15th. These facilities had sub-15% EBITDA margins amid 65% Medicaid mix, high uncompensated care (8% of revenue), and negative volume trends from rural depopulation. Post-sale, our portfolio EBITDA margin expands 50 basis points to 26.2%, and we retained the employed physician feeder practices.

Pipeline includes one more divestiture: a $115 million sale of our underutilized long-term acute care hospital in West Texas, LOI signed, closing Q1 2025. This 120-bed facility's margins eroded to 12% on flat ventilator days and rising contract labor at 25% of payroll. Proceeds will fund ASC tuck-ins, reflecting industry trends—LTAC utilization down 18% since 2019 per Definitive Healthcare data—as payers steer to skilled nursing facilities and home health.

Overall, M&A is turbocharging our 2024 guidance: inorganic revenue now embedded at +$900 million, lifting full-year growth to 11-13%. Synergies year-to-date hit $65 million, on track for $110 million, primarily from supply chain (35%), IT standardization (25%), and revenue cycle (20%). Risks include regulatory scrutiny on market share in MSAs over 30%, but our HHI scores remain below DOJ thresholds, and we're modeling 2-3% reimbursement headwinds from site-neutral policies.

Strategically, this positions us like peers—HCA's 15-hospital add-ons and Tenet's ASC pivot—but with a HealthBridge edge: 70% of deals EPS-accretive Day 1 via our $4.5 billion liquidity and 3.2x net debt/EBITDA. We're betting on consolidation: Hospital M&A volume up 25% year-over-year per Bain, driven by $100 billion-plus in seller liquidity needs from legacy operators like Community Health Systems. Forward-looking, expect 2-3 closes in Q4, $1.5-2 billion deployed in 2025, targeting 30% outpatient revenue mix by 2027.

Shifting to the impact of seasonality or external factors, particularly flu season, which played a significant role as we head into Q4. Q4 represents our peak flu season, aligning with CDC data showing national influenza-like illness activity hitting high levels from mid-December through February. For HealthBridge, this translated to a 14% sequential increase in emergency department volumes from Q3, reaching 1.2 million visits across our 180 acute care hospitals in 28 states. Inpatient admissions surged 12% quarter-over-quarter, with average daily census climbing to 85% utilization—our highest in three years—primarily from pneumonia and acute respiratory distress cases. This volume lift added approximately $175 million to our net patient revenue, or about 7% of our quarterly top line, net of bad debt and contractual allowances.

Year-over-year, flu-driven volumes were up 9%, outpacing the 5% national hospital admission growth reported by the American Hospital Association. Our case mix index rose to 1.85 from 1.78 in Q4 2022, reflecting a higher acuity mix—such as more Medicare DRG 207s for respiratory system diagnoses with major complications or comorbidities, which command reimbursement rates 20-30% above average under the IPPS. Payer mix held steady at 52% Medicare, 28% commercial, and 15% Medicaid, but we saw a favorable shift with Medicare Advantage penetration increasing to 22% of Medicare lives, thanks to value-based care contracts with Humana and UnitedHealthcare.

Regionally, the impact was uneven. In our Northeast markets—Boston, Philly, and upstate New York—flu cases spiked 22% year-over-year, per state health department data, pushing ED wait times to 210 minutes on peak days and straining our footprint there. This led to a 15% EBITDA margin expansion in those facilities to 18.5%, but it came at the cost of overtime premiums eating 3% into departmental expenses. Contrast that with our Sunbelt regions like Texas and Florida, where milder winters tempered flu activity to just a 6% volume bump; here, we leaned on outpatient services, with ambulatory surgery centers offsetting any inpatient softness by ramping orthopedics and cataracts deferred from summer.

External factors amplified this seasonality. Harsh winter storms across the Midwest delayed 8% of elective procedures—hip/knee replacements and cardiac caths—mirroring trends at peers like HCA Healthcare. On the positive side, RSV and COVID co-circulation boosted pediatric volumes by 18% in our children's hospitals, adding $25 million in specialized revenue. Vaccination rates helped mitigate severity; our system-wide flu shot program, in partnership with Sanofi and Seqirus, achieved 68% staff coverage and 55% patient uptake in high-risk clinics, reducing average length of stay for influenza cases to 4.2 days from 4.8 last year.

Our strategic response includes heavy investment in predictive analytics via our enterprise command center, powered by Epic's SlicerDicer and Google Cloud AI, which forecasted a 12% flu surge three weeks ahead this season with 92% accuracy. This allowed us to flex staffing via our Workforce Management platform, surging RN hours by 11% through float pools and travel contracts without spiking agency costs above 6% of payroll—down from 9% in FY22 amid the post-COVID labor crunch. We also expanded tele-ICU capabilities, handling 25% of respiratory monitoring remotely, which preserved 150 beds for higher-margin cases.

On the capex front, we're allocating $50 million in FY24 to regional surge pods—modular 20-bed units deployable in 48 hours, similar to Tenet Healthcare's rapid-response model. Long-term, our shift to site-neutral payments under the CMS Outpatient Prospective Payment System will derisk elective seasonality, targeting 15% of revenue from hospital-at-home programs by 2025, inspired by Mayo Clinic's successful rollout.

Looking forward, we expect Q1 flu tailwinds to fade into spring, with volumes normalizing to 2-3% year-over-year growth absent another surge. However, with an aging demographic—Medicare enrollees up 4% nationally—and potential CMS cuts to the 2024 IPPS conversion factor by 2.9%, we'll prioritize case mix index expansion and cost discipline. Our FY24 EBITDA guidance of $1.15-1.20 billion embeds a conservative 5% seasonality adder, positioning us for 10%+ margin expansion.

Finally, trends in staffing levels and contract labor usage, one of our key operational levers. Labor expenses represent about 55% of our total operating costs, making staffing optimization mission-critical for margin expansion in this high-fixed-cost industry.

Post-pandemic, the healthcare labor market has seen an acute shortage-driven surge in contract labor from 2020 to mid-2022, followed by gradual normalization as burnout eases and retention improves. At our peak in Q2 2022, contract labor—primarily travel nurses and allied health professionals sourced through partners like AMN Healthcare and Cross Country Healthcare—accounted for 18% of our total nursing workforce and drove contract expenses to $285 million, or 12% of consolidated revenue. That was a 250% sequential spike from pre-COVID levels, fueled by RN turnover rates hitting 25% industry-wide, per NSI Nursing Solutions data, and exacerbated by California-mandated nurse-to-patient ratios under AB 394.

Fast-forward to Q3 this year: Total system-wide FTEs stand at 42,500, up 4% year-over-year and flat sequentially, reflecting disciplined hiring aligned with our 2.5% adjusted admission growth. Contract labor usage has de-escalated dramatically to just 5.2% of nursing hours, down from 9.8% in Q3 2023 and an 85% reduction from our 2022 peak. This translates to contract expenses of $62 million in the quarter—about 3% of revenue—saving us $45 million sequentially and $120 million year-to-date versus prior-year comparables. On a trailing 12-month basis, labor costs as a percentage of net patient revenue have compressed 210 basis points to 52.8%, directly contributing 150 basis points to our operating margin expansion.

Breaking it down by caregiver cadre: Registered nurses remain our largest cohort at 18,200 FTEs, or 43% of total staff. RN contract penetration is now 4.1%, versus 15% a year ago, thanks to our RN retention rate climbing to 87% from 72%—outpacing the Vizient median of 82%. We've added 650 net new permanent RNs quarter-over-quarter, focused on high-acuity specialties like ICU and OR, where work relative value units per nurse have risen 8% to 4,200 on better scheduling efficiency. For aides and techs, contract usage is negligible at under 2%, as we've leaned into CNA academies in partnership with local community colleges. Physician staffing—1,200 FTE equivalents via employed and aligned models—saw a 3% uptick, bolstered by our Fair Market Value-aligned incentives, which have stabilized coverage amid the ongoing primary care shortage projected by AAMC to hit 86,000 by 2036.

Regionally, the story varies. In our high-growth Sunbelt markets—Texas and Florida, representing 45% of bed capacity—staffing levels are up 7% year-over-year, with contract reliance at a low 3.5%. Facilities like our new 300-bed freestanding ER-hospital hybrid in the Dallas-Fort Worth MSA are staffing at 105% of target, capitalizing on inbound migration and lower regulatory burdens. This contrasts with our legacy Northeast and Midwest markets (30% of capacity), where urban density and union pressures have kept contracts at 7-8%, though even there, we've cut usage 40% year-over-year through localized retention bonuses averaging $25,000 per RN. Rural facilities, 25% of our footprint akin to Community Health Systems' model, face the steepest headwinds with 12% contract penetration due to reimbursement gaps under the Medicare 340B program, but our tele-ICU partnerships with Teleflex are stretching existing staff, reducing on-site needs by 15%.

Strategically, we're accelerating normalization through our $75 million Workforce 2025 program, launched last year, which includes sign-on bonuses tiered by market (up to $50K in tight spots like Chicago), tuition reimbursement via the Nurse Corps Loan Repayment tie-ins, and a 15% average wage uplift for tenured staff, now averaging $112K base for RNs. Tech deployment: We've rolled out AI-driven scheduling via ShiftMed and Epic's MySchedule module across 85% of facilities, optimizing fill rates to 96% and cutting overtime 22%. Predictive analytics from our Oracle Health EHR integration forecast staffing needs 30 days out, correlating to a 10% drop in per-admission labor costs. We're de-risking via contingent workforce frameworks with AMN and Favorite Staffing, shifting to rapid response contracts that cap rates at 1.5x permanent pay, versus the 2.5x peaks of 2022.

Looking forward, we expect contract labor to trend toward 3-4% of nursing hours by year-end 2025, assuming no major flu/COVID resurgence, with total FTE growth of 2-3% tied to our 3-4% adjusted admission guidance. This should deliver another 100-150 basis points of labor margin relief, positioning us competitively against peers like HCA.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Dr. Kline for an update on our clinical initiatives.

Dr. Robert Kline:
Thank you, Jennifer. Good morning. We are making significant progress in improving clinical outcomes and patient satisfaction. Our PatientSync Care Coordination program has shown promising results, with an 18% reduction in readmission rates. We are also focused on leveraging technology to enhance the patient experience and improve care coordination, including advanced telehealth integrations and AI predictive tools for personalized treatment pathways.

Now, I'd like to turn the call back to Dr. Reynolds.

Dr. Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Dr. Kline. At this time, we will open the call for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on the impact of the da Vinci Xi robotic systems on your revenue growth and the impact on hospital efficiency?

Dr. Michael Reynolds:
Good morning, John. Great question. The da Vinci Xi systems have been transformative, now deployed across 75% of our facilities and driving 15% growth in joint replacement volumes. They've boosted our case mix index by capturing higher-acuity procedures, contributing about 1% to revenue per admission growth this quarter. On efficiency, they've shortened length of stay by 0.3 days on average and increased OR throughput by 12%, directly supporting our margin expansion. We're on track to expand to 85% coverage next year.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
What are your plans for expanding your network of hospitals and clinics in the coming year?

David Patel:
Thanks, Lisa. Our expansion strategy blends organic growth and M&A. Organically, we're adding 50 beds in key Sunbelt markets like Dallas-Fort Worth and scaling hospital-at-home to 15 sites. On the inorganic side, as Jennifer outlined, we're closing the Coastal Ambulatory Partners deal by year-end and advancing the Heartland bid, targeting 2-3 deals in Q4 and $1.5-2 billion deployed in 2025. This will grow our footprint to over 200 hospitals while hitting 30% outpatient mix by 2027.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Rodriguez with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mike Rodriguez:
Can you elaborate on the specific technologies you are implementing to improve care coordination?

Dr. Robert Kline:
Absolutely, Mike. We're leveraging Epic's SlicerDicer for predictive analytics, integrated with Google Cloud AI to forecast patient needs and reduce readmissions. Our BridgeConnect telehealth platform handles 25% of consults, expanding catchment areas, while Nuance Dragon and tele-ICU tools enable remote monitoring, cutting on-site staffing needs by 15%. These have improved STAR ratings to 92% in value-based contracts.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Grant with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Grant:
Thanks. On the staffing trends, how sustainable is the contract labor reduction, and any risks from flu season?

Jennifer Lee:
Hi Emily. The reduction to 5.2% is sustainable, driven by our Workforce 2025 program and 87% RN retention. We've capped rapid-response contracts at 1.5x permanent pay. Flu season risks are managed via predictive scheduling—fill rates at 96%—and surge pods, keeping agency under 6% of payroll even in peaks.

Dr. Michael Reynolds:
